newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada sees no action at Stuttgart talks on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Canada sees no action at Stuttgart talks on Zaire.

text.p: A meeting in Stuttgart on Friday of military planners on the Zaire crisis will not make any decisions whether to send a force, Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Thursday.
"There will not be a decision in Stuttgart. It is a meeting to look at all the factors and all the options, and after that there will be a context for a decision," Axworthy told reporters.
The problem seems to be chiefly a lack of clarity on the situation, given the difficulty aid workers have had in penetrating eastern Zaire to gauge refugee needs.
Canadian Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril, head of the U.N.-authorised mission, has been gathering information and holding discussions with central African governments.
Officials had suggested that at the Stuttgart talks -- originally set for Wednesday -- he would shape the mission with other countries which have agreed to participate.
Some agencies have begun to express alarm at the possibility that the force might not even go, given the exodus to Rwanda of half a million refugees.

"We understand that the mission may need to be modified in light of the refugee movements over the weekend, but we cannot forget that over half-a-million refugees are still inaccessible inside Zaire," said CARE Canada, one of the agencies mandated to distribute aid.

"Many refugees are still cut off and unable to cross the border. We need to create humanitarian corridors, safe havens and delivery mechanisms to reach these people, and we need the help of the Canadian-led force to do it."
Axworthy said countries meeting in New York on Wednesday renewed their support for a mission "if necessary."
"And that's the key word, that there'll be a military force if necessary, not necessarily that there'll be a force if the need disappears," he said.
Asked when a decision would be made on how to proceed with the Canadian-led rescue mission, he said: "Soon...We'll make the decisions when we can."

Axworthy said strategists were still trying to gather information, through reconnaissance flights and other means, to get a clearer picture of needs after the exodus to Rwanda of half a million refugees a week ago.
"I don't think anyone would want us to make a decision without the right information and having some degree of certainty," he said.
